newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba reinforces patrols to monitor exile plans.
newsitem.headline: Cuba reinforces patrols to monitor exile plans.

text.p: Cuba reinforced coast guard patrols on Monday to stop any violation of its territory by Miami-based exiles planning to mark the anniversary of the downing of two of their planes by Cuban MiG fighters one year ago.
Several dozen local and foreign reporters were taken out to sea on a coast guard submarine chaser. It was not clear how many other vessels would take part in patrols.
The Cuban Foreign Ministry, warning exile groups it would not tolerate territorial violations, said last week Cuba would use any means necesary to prevent such violations.

Exile groups in Miami planned to fly planes over the Florida Straits to throw flowers over the sea off Cuba's north's coast where the two small Cessna planes, operated by an exile group called Brothers to the Rescue, were shot down on Feb. 24, 1996.
The incident, in which the four flyers were killed, sparked international outrage against Cuba and prompted Washington to toughened its longstanding economic embargo on Cuba.
President Fidel Castro's government said it acted in legitimate self-defence. It said the planes were in Cuban airspace when they were shot down and ignored warnings to leave.
Washington said the downings were an act of brutality. It said the planes were over international waters and, wherever they were, should not have been shot down.

The names of the four exiles killed in the incident were read out and remembered during a mass on Monday morning at one Havana church. The names, part of a customary list of people to be mourned, were apparently included by relatives.

Cuban authorities reiterated Monday that the plane downings could have been prevented by the United States. An article in the weekly newspaper Trabajadores said Washington should have acted to prevent territorial violations by Cuban exile groups.

The newspaper noted that Cuba had clearly warned in January 1996 that it might use force to prevent territorial violations. It added that U.S. authorities had been fully aware of the situation and of the exile group's plans, but had not acted.

The public warning by Cuba that it might use force was issued on Jan. 15, 1996, following incidents one week before when anti-government leaflets were scattered over Havana by Brothers to the Rescue planes.
Havana said at the time its patience was running out after numerous violations of its territory over the previous 20 months.
Brothers to the Rescue president Jose Basulto has said the leaflets were scattered from outside Cuba's 12-mile territorial limit and winds carried them over Cuba.
